Chapter Three: The Struggle Between Oppression and the Desire for Freedom.
As we move deeper into these poems, something new starts to surface. There’s this powerful tension—almost like a tug-of-war—between control and the very real longing to break free.
You see, the world painted in these verses isn’t just tough. It’s unfair, shaped by those holding all the power. The poems start to focus in on the systems and rules that keep people boxed in, often without them even realizing it.
Picture this: a worker, rising before the sun, hands rough and calloused from endless labor. The day ahead feels endless, stacked with tasks that never really seem to finish. But here’s the thing—their exhaustion runs deeper than tired muscles. It’s a weariness of the spirit, a heavy sense that life’s being lived for someone else’s gain. These lines capture that quiet struggle, showing how oppression can seep into every part of daily life.
Then, there’s a poem about a child who dreams of running wild through open fields, but instead, is kept inside by strict parents. You can really feel the child’s longing—it’s a mix of frustration and hope, all tangled together. The rules are supposed to protect, but they end up smothering, too. What’s striking is, the poem doesn’t point fingers at the parents. Instead, it gently reveals how fear can make us build walls, even around those we care about most.
Some poems look outward, at the ways society pushes everyone to fit in, to play a role, to stick to a script someone else wrote. If you step out of line? You’re either ignored, or worse, punished. And these poems don’t just tell you about that pressure—they make you feel it. There’s this weight of expectation, pressing down, making it hard to breathe.
But here’s something beautiful—no matter how heavy things get, that desire for freedom never really fades. The poems are dotted with small acts of rebellion: a child sneaking out just to see the stars, a worker pausing for a moment to listen to birdsong. These moments are brief, but they matter so much. They’re reminders that the human spirit is tough to crush. Even in the darkest times, people find ways to hold onto their dignity.
There’s another idea woven through these verses: real freedom isn’t just about breaking rules. It’s about picturing a different kind of life, one where kindness and creativity matter more than simply obeying. The poems invite us to question the systems we take for granted, to ask—does it really have to be this way?
By the end of this section, something big starts to happen. The poems shift from showing us individual struggles to hinting at a much larger feeling—a shared yearning for change. They might not promise a revolution, but they do offer a glimpse of what’s possible, if we’re brave enough to imagine it.
So, if you’re feeling the weight of expectations, or the walls closing in, remember: these poems are a quiet call to dream—together—of something better.
